scenes.tts: Run up a flight of stairs. Your heart pounds faster. Then, over the next few minutes, it slows again. On a hot, dry afternoon, tiny pores on the underside of many leaves narrow. The world outside keeps changing. How do living things keep their insides steady?
scenes.visual: A heart block pulses fast then slow; a leaf pore narrows; both fold into an inside box hit by outside arrows, with a question mark.
scenes.narration: Run up a flight of stairs. Your heart pounds faster. Then, over the next few minutes, it slows again. On a hot, dry afternoon, tiny pores on the underside of many leaves narrow. The world outside keeps changing. How do living things keep their insides steady?

scenes.tts: Biologists call this homeostasis. Homeostasis means keeping internal conditions within a stable range, while the outside changes. The word range matters. Your body temperature is usually near 37 degrees Celsius. But it shifts a little through the day. It is not fixed at one number.
scenes.caption: Biologists call this homeostasis. Homeostasis means keeping internal conditions within a stable range, while the outside changes. The word range matters. Your body temperature is usually near 37 °C. But it shifts a little through the day. It is not fixed at one number.
scenes.visual: A wobbling line stays inside a green band labelled stable range.
scenes.narration: Biologists call this homeostasis. Homeostasis means keeping internal conditions within a stable range, while the outside changes. The word range matters. Your body temperature is usually near 37 °C. But it shifts a little through the day. It is not fixed at one number.

scenes.tts: Most homeostasis works by negative feedback. In negative feedback, the response opposes the change that started it. Negative does not mean bad. It means the response pushes the other way. So when a variable drifts up, the response pushes it down.
scenes.visual: The line drifts up out of the band; a response arrow pushes it down and back into the band.
scenes.narration: Most homeostasis works by negative feedback. In negative feedback, the response opposes the change that started it. Negative does not mean bad. It means the response pushes the other way. So when a variable drifts up, the response pushes it down.

scenes.tts: Every loop has the same parts. First, a change pushes a variable away from its usual range. A sensor is a cell or organ that detects the change. The control center compares it with the usual range, and sends a signal. In your body, this is usually the brain. An effector is a muscle, gland, or cell that carries out the response.
scenes.visual: Five labelled blocks join in a loop: change, sensor, control center, effector, response.
scenes.narration: Every loop has the same parts. First, a change pushes a variable away from its usual range. A sensor is a cell or organ that detects the change. The control center compares it with the usual range, and sends a signal. In your body, this is usually the brain. An effector is a muscle, gland, or cell that carries out the response.

scenes.tts: Here is the loop on a hot day. Your body warms. Temperature sensors in the skin and brain detect it. The control center in the brain sends a signal. Sweat glands release sweat. The sweat evaporates, and the skin cools. That response pushes the change back.
scenes.visual: The loop blocks take the hot-day labels one by one while a temperature bar rises, then comes down.
scenes.narration: Here is the loop on a hot day. Your body warms. Temperature sensors in the skin and brain detect it. The control center in the brain sends a signal. Sweat glands release sweat. The sweat evaporates, and the skin cools. That response pushes the change back.

scenes.tts: Plants respond too. A leaf has tiny pores called stomata. Each pore sits between two guard cells. The guard cells change shape to open or narrow it. Dry air makes a leaf lose water faster. In drier air, guard cells can close the pores, which slows water loss. So how do living things stay steady inside? They sense a change. Then they respond in a way that pushes it back.
scenes.visual: A leaf cross-section block: guard cells narrow the pore; then the answer chain sense, respond, push back.
